'''Bridgefy''' is a Mexican software company with offices in Mexico<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=2 February 2021|title=Mexican-based startup.|url=https://www.freemalaysiatoday.com/category/business/2021/02/02/myanmar-skirts-internet-shutdown-with-mexican-app/}}</ref> and California, the United States, dedicated to developing mesh-networking technology for mobile apps. It was founded circa 2014 by Jorge Rios, Roberto Betancourt and Diego Garcia who conceived the idea while participating in a tech competition called [[StartupBus]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Bridgefy, la startup mexicana que te dejará pedir un Uber o recibir una alerta sísmica sin internet|trans-title=Bridgefy, the Mexican startup that will let you call an Uber or receive a seismic alert without the Internet|first=Franck|last=Velázquez|work=[[Entrepreneur (magazine)|Entrepreneur]]|date=November 22, 2018|language=Spanish|url=https://www.entrepreneur.com/article/323675|access-date=September 4, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190904030219/https://www.entrepreneur.com/article/323675|archive-date=September 4, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> Bridgefy's [[smartphone ad hoc network]] technology, apparently using [[Bluetooth mesh networking|Bluetooth Mesh]], is licensed to other apps.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://qz.com/1701045/hong-kong-protestors-use-bridgefy-to-preempt-internet-shutdown/|title=Hong Kong protestors revive mesh networks to preempt internet shutdown|last=Silva|first=Matthew |language=en|access-date=2019-09-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190903211212/https://qz.com/1701045/hong-kong-protestors-use-bridgefy-to-preempt-internet-shutdown/|archive-date=2019-09-03|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.indiatimes.com/technology/news/hong-kong-protestors-are-using-an-app-that-doesn-t-need-internet-and-bypass-chinese-snooping-374969.html|title=Hong Kong Protestors Are Using An App That Doesn't Need Internet, And Bypass Chinese Snooping|date=2019-09-03|newspaper=The Times of India|language=en|access-date=2019-09-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190903211212/https://www.indiatimes.com/technology/news/hong-kong-protestors-are-using-an-app-that-doesn-t-need-internet-and-bypass-chinese-snooping-374969.html|archive-date=2019-09-03|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite The app gained popularity during protests in different countries since it can operate without Internet, using Bluetooth instead. Aware of the security issues of not using cryptography and the criticism surrounding it,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Goodin|first=Dan|date=2020-08-24|title=Bridgefy, the messenger promoted for mass protests, is a privacy disaster|url=https://arstechnica.com/features/2020/08/bridgefy-the-app-promoted-for-mass-protests-is-a-privacy-disaster/|access-date=2020-08-26|website=Ars Technica|language=en-us}}</ref> Bridgefy announced in late October 2020 that they adopted the [[Signal Protocol|Signal protocol]], in both their app and SDK, to keep information private,<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Press Release – Major Security Updates at Bridgefy!|url=https://bridgefy.me/press-release-major-security-updates-at-bridgefy/|access-date=2021-04-27|website=Bridgefy|language=en-US|archive-date=2021-12-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211214163819/https://bridgefy.me/press-release-major-security-updates-at-bridgefy/|url-status=dead}}</ref> though security researchers have demonstrated that Bridgefy's usage of the Signal Protocol is insecure.<ref name="breaking-bridgefy-again-github">{{cite web |last1=Eikenberg |first1=Raphael |title=Breaking Bridgefy, again |url=https://eikendev.github.io/breaking-bridgefy-again/ |publisher=GitHub |access-date=14 June 2022}}</ref>

==Usage==
The app gained popularity [[Tactics and methods surrounding the 2019–2020 Hong Kong protests#Peer-to-peer mesh broadcasting|as a communication tactic]] during the [[2019–2020 Hong Kong protests]] and [[Citizenship Amendment Act protests]] in India,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.livemint.com/technology/apps/bridgefy-an-offline-messaging-app-suddenly-gaining-traction-in-india-11576766348376.html|title=Bridgefy: An offline messaging app suddenly gaining traction in India|last=Nandi|first=Tamal|date=2019-12-19|website=livemint.com|language=en|access-date=2019-12-22}}</ref> because it requires people who want to intercept the message to be physically close because of Bluetooth's limited range, and the ability to daisy-chain devices to send messages further than Bluetooth's range.<ref>{{Cite == Security ==
In August 2020, researchers published a paper describing numerous attacks against the application, which allow de-anonymizing users, building social graphs of users’ interactions (both in real time and after the fact), decrypting and reading direct messages, impersonating users to anyone else on the network, completely shutting down the network, performing active [[man-in-the-middle attack]]s to read messages and even modify them.<ref name=":0" />

In response to the disclosures, developers acknowledged that "no part of the Bridgefy app is encrypted now" and gave a vague promise to release a new version "encrypted with top security protocols".<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Bridgefly: No part of the Bridgefy app is encrypted now.|url=https://twitter.com/bridgefy/status/1268551771124834313|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200604144136/https://twitter.com/bridgefy/status/1268551771124834313 |archive-date=2020-06-04 |access-date=2020-08-26|website=Twitter|language=en}}</ref> Later developers said they plan to switch to [[Signal Protocol]], which is widely recognized by cryptographers and used by [[Signal (messaging app)|Signal]] and [[WhatsApp]].<ref name=":0" /> The Signal Protocol was integrated into the Bridgefy app and SDK by late October 2020, with the developers claiming to have included improvements such as the impossibility of a third person impersonating any other user, man-in-the-middle attacks done by modifying stored keys, and historical proximity tracking, among others.<ref name=":1" />

However, in 2022, the same security researchers, now including [[Kenny Paterson]], published a paper describing how Bridgefy's usage of the Signal Protocol was incorrect, failing to remedy the previously discovered issues.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Albrecht |first1=Martin R. |last2=Eikenberg |first2=Raphael |last3=Paterson |first3=Kenneth G. |title=Breaking Bridgefy, again |journal=USENIX Security |date=2022 |issue=22 |isbn=9781939133311 |url=https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity22/presentation/albrecht |access-date=14 June 2022 |ref=breaking-bridgefy-again-usenix}}</ref> The researchers performed a demonstration, showing that it was possible for users to intercept messages intended for others without the sender noticing.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Eikenberg |first1=Raphael |title=Breaking Bridgefy again attack demo |url=https://twitter.com/eikendev/status/1427542406262575105 |website=Twitter |access-date=14 June 2022 |ref=breaking-bridgefy-again-demo}}</ref> The researchers disclosed the vulnerabilities to the developers of Bridgefy in August 2021, but, according to the researchers, the developers had yet to resolve the issues as of June 2022.<ref name="breaking-bridgefy-again-github" />

On July 31, 2023, the security firm [[7asecurity]] released a [https://7asecurity.com/blog/2023/07/bridgefy-audit/ blog post] and [https://7asecurity.com/reports/pentest-report-bridgefy.pdf pentest report] of a white box [[penetration test]] and overall security review of the Bridgefy app in collaboration with the platform's developers. Their review, which began in November 2022 and concluded in May 2023, identified multiple critical vulnerabilities throughout the application. Many of the issues were fixed, or partially fixed, before the end of the audit, including user impersonation and [[Biometric authentication|biometric]] bypass. Bridgefy also [https://bridgefy.me/blog/security-audit/ published a blog post] on August 8, 2023, announcing the audit results.
